newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada says Zaire refugee mission remains vital.
newsitem.headline: Canada says Zaire refugee mission remains vital.

text.p: An international humanitarian mission in central Africa, instigated by Canada, will go ahead despite a mass return of Rwandan refugees from Zaire, a spokeswoman for Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Friday.
"It's all systems go. We're still continuing with the plans for the mission as planned," spokeswoman Leslie Swartman told Reuters. "It certainly doesn't mean there's an end to the crisis there."

The United Nations estimates that up to 400,000 refugees suddenly began trekking back to Rwanda from the vast Mugunga camp in eastern Zaire on Friday, but U.N. officials say hundreds of thousands of refugees remain.
"It's very positive," Swartman said, but she added: "There is still a crisis happening and we're going ahead as planned."

Chretien personally spearheaded creation of the U.N. force, offering Canadian leadership and phoning leaders around the world to end U.N. delays. Canadian Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril, former military adviser on peacekeeping to Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, will head the force and Chretien's nephew Raymond is the U.N. envoy for the crisis.

Three C-130 Hercules transport planes left for the region on Thursday and Friday from the Trenton military base in Ontario with about 30 reconnaissance personnel on board, Canadian spokesman Capt. Ian Stock said by phone from Trenton.
"They're strictly an advance reconnaissance team," Stock said, adding they would provide information to assist in preparing the multinational force.
Most of the space in the transport planes was taken up with small trucks. A further flight of up to 100 reconnnaissance troops was tentatively scheduled for Saturday.
Chretien was trying to read a novel at his Harrington Lake retreat outside Ottawa last Saturday when he became disturbed by television pictures of the refugees, Swartman said.

He began phoning around the world -- from South African President Nelson Mandela to Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso -- and his aides laid the groundwork for a conversation with U.S. President Bill Clinton. Chretien finally talked with him on Monday morning, a few hours before Clinton made the crucial announcement that Washington would agree in principle to participate.

Canadian foreign affairs spokesman John Bell said that despite the return of many refugees hundreds of thousands remained in Zaire. "The situation is still precarious on the ground for refugees," he said, adding that eastern Zairean airports at Goma and Bukuvu were still not secure and could not be used properly to deliver aid.
